title: Why Having Fun Makes Classroom Management Easier ment-easier/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin recalls team-teaching a summer school science class alongside a colleague named John, who ran his classroom with no formal classroom management plan yet still produced well-behaved students, largely because his lessons were so much fun that students wanted to meet his expectations. Linsin uses this story to argue that enjoyment is not a frill in classroom management but genuine leverage: students who are happy to be in school learn and behave better than those who are not. He cautions that fun alone is imperfect without a plan and rules, but paired together, an exciting learning environment and a willingness to enforce consequences form what he calls the keys to the kingdom. The piece closes with a simple charge to teachers: schedule learning games, tell stories, be your silly self, and occasionally make a fool of yourself for the sake of your students.
points: A teacher who is genuinely fun to be around gains cooperation students would not otherwise give.
Fun without a classroom management plan works imperfectly; fun combined with a plan is far more powerful.
Students who enjoy being in school demonstrably learn and behave better than those who do not.
Simple, low-effort gestures — games, stories, humor, self-deprecation — build meaningful leverage over time.
quotes: There is no getting around the fact that students who are happy to be in school, learn and behave better than those who don’t. It makes perfect sense, yet many teachers miss this simple truth.

It occurred to me in that moment that John was teaching without a net (i.e., no classroom management plan). Although he was quick to correct students who interfered with learning, he didn’t seem to have any specified rules or consequences.
John wasted a lot of time and energy reminding students of this and that and asking for quiet so he could speak—which could have been avoided if he had had a classroom management plan.

John was so much fun, and his lessons so interesting, that his students would have done anything to be a part of his class, including behaving in whatever manner he deemed acceptable—however unspecified that was.
Adding some fun to your classroom isn’t difficult. It doesn’t take a lot of pre-planning and you don’t need any special talent. It just takes a willingness to make it a priority.
Your students will appreciate it, and you’ll add more leverage to your classroom management plan.
